claims.text: Adding 0.5–1.0 at% B with controlled thermal processing will produce boride precipitates in a MoNbTaW-based refractory high-entropy alloy.
The resulting boride precipitates will be nanoscale, coherent, and uniformly distributed.
Boride precipitates will occur both within the matrix and at grain boundaries.
The precipitates will strengthen the alloy by pinning dislocations.
Precipitates at grain boundaries will inhibit grain-boundary sliding during high-temperature deformation.
Limiting the B addition to 0.5–1.0 at% will minimize the change in alloy density.
The limited B addition and controlled precipitate population will preserve room-temperature microstructure and ductility.
Relative to undoped MoNbTaW, the B-modified alloy will improve high-temperature creep resistance by approximately 20–30%.
Relative to undoped MoNbTaW, the B-modified alloy will improve high-temperature tensile strength by approximately 20–30%.
The predicted mechanical improvement will hold at 1000–1200 °C under static and cyclic loading.
The B-modified alloy will retain room-temperature strength and ductility relative to the undoped baseline.
The B addition will cause a negligible density increase of less than 1%.
Failure to control precipitate size and coherence may produce coarse or incoherent precipitates that embrittle the alloy at room temperature.
A prior Hf-addition study found that an Hf0.5 alloy had greater strength and ductility than an Hf0 alloy at 600, 800, and 900 °C.

In the prior Hf-addition study, high-temperature strength was attributed to precipitation strengthening by an Hf-rich phase, and high-temperature ductility was attributed to boundary pinning that resisted sliding.
The undoped MoNbTaW baseline has a homogeneous microstructure.
